historical_claims.anchor: Jacques Dixmier was born in Saint-Étienne, France, in May of nineteen twenty-four.
Dixmier entered the École Normale Supérieure in Paris in nineteen forty-two, under German occupation.
A few days before the liberation of Paris in August nineteen forty-four, Gestapo officers came to the École Normale.
Two teachers were particularly important to him: Henri Cartan and Gaston Julia.
Dixmier's thesis studied special linear sets of this kind.
historical_claims.source_locator: 1949 BSMF thesis title/contents; Dixmier p.36 on Julia varieties

historical_claims.anchor: In nineteen forty-eight he published a study of the relative position of two closed linear subspaces in a Hilbert space.
One is often called the Dixmier angle, or minimal angle.
For two closed subspaces, a positive Friedrichs angle is equivalent to the closedness of their sum.
Halmos explicitly credited Dixmier with an earlier theorem classifying pairs of subspaces up to unitary equivalence
His nineteen forty-nine paper on finite-class rings of operators is a major early step in this direction.
historical_claims.source_locator: 1949 Ann. Sci. ENS article metadata and references

historical_claims.anchor: Dixmier met von Neumann briefly in Paris in nineteen forty-seven.
Dixmier gave the credit to Jean Dieudonné, who proposed it during a Bourbaki discussion.

historical_claims.anchor: Dixmier's nineteen sixty-four book on C-star algebras and their representations was part of the consolidation of this field.

historical_claims.anchor: Dixmier joined the Bourbaki group in nineteen forty-nine, after Jean-Pierre Serre and Pierre Samuel invited him.
In the interview, he explained that he prepared mathematical talks word for word.
His students included Alain Connes, Michel Duflo, and Michèle Vergne.
Dixmier retired at sixty, in nineteen eighty-four, under a law that allowed retirement at that age.
